1.text: “STRONG MEN.” — The word “eˊrmečɪn” was mentioned in the previous

2.text: chapter as designating the master of the camp. It signifies literally “the

3.text: strongest one,” and is used with several other meanings, which are of course

4.text: more or less closely related. These are “the strong man,” “the warrior,”

5.text: “the influential man,” “the violent man,” “the robber.” The Chukchee are

6.text: conscious of the difference between the meanings of the word. For instance,

7.text: a quotation from the tale of “Eleˊndi and His Sons,” given in the preceding

8.text: chapter,¹ contains a pun founded on this difference of meaning. The Eskimo

9.text: host says, “This is probably the well-known Reindeer Chukchee eˊrmečɪn”

10.text: (meaning warrior). Eleˊndi answers, “Not I. Only you are the real eˊrmečɪn

11.text: (meaning violent man), because by violence you so taught your neighbors that

12.text: they do not dare to eat in your presence.” But if this quotation shows a

13.text: marked difference between the two meanings of the word, another quotation

14.text: from the latter part of the same tale, on the contrary, points out the common

15.text: element of all these notions, — warlike strength. “Oh, oh!” says the father,

16.text: after his young son has made a very successful shot, “then I have created a

17.text: future violent man, a robber of the herds of all other people, a warrior I have

18.text: created. I am a good man.”

19.text: In the original text the word “eˊrmečɪn” was used in all three cases.

20.text: War and warriors belong to the past life of the Chukchee tribe. Therefore they

21.text: are described only in tales and other narratives of the same character. In

22.text: modern life, by “eˊrmečɪn” is meant, first of all, a man of great physical

23.text: strength, daring temper, and adventurous disposition. Men with such qualities

24.text: may be met among the Chukchee, both Reindeer and Maritime. Such, for

25.text: instance, was one of my Kolyma acquaintances, Tŭmg̣änêˊntɪ by name. He

26.text: was of Maritime origin, but lived among the Reindeer people from early youth.

27.text: Tŭmg̣änêˊntɪ was a man of tall stature and athletic build, and experienced

28.text: in all kinds of sports, wrestling, running, racing with reindeer. When I met

29.text: him, he was about forty, and more or less quiet; but his previous life had

30.text: been quite eventful. Being of Maritime origin he has visited most of the

31.text: Arctic villages, and quite a number of camps on the route between East

32.text: Cape and the Kolyma River. He tried to be a trader; but he squandered

33.text: most of his wares, and had to give up his attempts. Two or three times he

34.text: was the owner of a large herd, but each time it was gone again after a year

35.text: or two. He was much given to drink; and when drunk, his temper was

36.text: quite dangerous. Thus he was said to have killed on different occasions
